items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public authorities law, in relation to the liability of a
municipality or governmental subdivision for the refund of property taxes to
the Long Island power authority
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5122

SPONSOR: GAUGHRAN
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the public authorities law, in
relation to the liability of a municipality or governmental subdivision
for the refund of property taxes to the Long Island power authority

 
PURPOSE:

The purpose of this bill is to limit the financial impact of adverse tax
certiorari challenges by LIPA on affected local governmental entities.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one adds a new subdivision four to section 1020-q of the public
authorities law. Parallel to the preceding subdivision, this provision
would limit the remedies available to LIPA when bringing tax certiorari
challenges by prohibiting relief in the form of repayment of all or part
of the taxes assessed against any power plant, transmission line or
substation from a prior year.

Section two provides that this act shall take effect thirty days after
becoming law.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

In 1998, LIPA acquired all the capital stock and associated assets of
Long Island Lighting Company (LILCO), which operated the electrical
system on Long Island. In connection with that acquisition, the authori-
ty took over ultimate responsibility for providing electric utility
service to residential, commercial, industrial, nonprofit and govern-
mental customers in the counties of Suffolk, Nassau and a portion of
Queens.

At the time of acquisition, then-Chariman Richard Kessel memorialized an
agreement that LIPA would never challenge the assessed values of their
properties, provided the municipalities never raised them. The devastat-
ing impact that tax-certiorari challenges would have on local govern-
mental entities was recognized from LIPA's inception.

In fact, at the time of acquisition the Shoreham Power Plant (through
LILCO), was challenging its tax assessment. To remedy this, a provision
was added to the enabling law governing LIPA providing that no refund of
taxes resulting from any judicial determination would be collected from
the impacted municipality (see Public Authorities Law 1020-q(3)).

Today, LIPA has initiated tax certiorari lawsuits across Long Island in
relation to various properties owned by the Authority. They are chal-
lenging their assessments for the current year, and seeking relief in
the form of a refund for taxes paid in prior years. This relief, if
granted, would be detrimental to the vitality of the communities in
which these properties are located and would have a direct impact on
their ability to provide indispensable programs and services. These
actions are in direct conflict with LIPA's enabling statute which
explicitly provides that the establishment of the authority will, among
other priorities, realize savings for the . . .  taxpayers in the
service area (see Public Authorities Law 1020-a).


This legislation would prevent LIPA for seeking relief in the form of a
return of past year tax payments, thereby limiting the financial hard-
ship that local governments would endure in the event of an adverse
judgment.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER: S5122A

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the public authorities law, in

mental entities was recognized from LIPA's inception.

In fact, at the time of acquisition the Shoreham Power Plant (through

This legislation would prevent LIPA for seeking relief in the form of a
return of past year tax payments, thereby limiting the financial hard-

New Bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
